title: Quantitative assay to detect bacterial glycan-degrading enzyme activities in mouse and human fecal samples
protocol: Prepare 100 mL of LB-PM buffer using kit component 4.
Remove 1 mL from the prepared LB-PM buffer.
Resuspend 1 aliquot of enzyme mix in the removed 1 mL of LB-PM buffer.
Transfer the resuspended enzyme mix back into the remaining LB-PM buffer.
If less than 100 mL is needed, adapt the volume of the enzyme solution accordingly.
Remove 1 mL of the enzyme mix-supplemented LB-PM buffer.
Resuspend 1 tablet of EDTA-free Protease inhibitor in the removed 1 mL volume.
Transfer the resuspended protease inhibitor back to the 100 mL of enzyme mix-supplemented LB-PM buffer.
Adapt the volume of protease inhibitor solution if less than 100 mL is needed for lysis.
Store the LB buffer on ice until further use.
Transfer approximately 20-100 mg of frozen (or freshly donated) human feces into a sonication device-compatible 1.5 mL tube and store on ice.
Add 500 μL of ice-cold LB buffer to the fecal sample, irrespective of the weight.
Homogenize the feces in the LB buffer using a pipette tip or an inoculation loop to break up large clumps.
Vortex the sample for 10 seconds.
Perform pulsed sonication at the highest available frequency for 15 seconds at a time, pausing for at least 10 seconds between each step.
Apply a total sonication time of 45 seconds while keeping samples on ice during and between sonication steps.
Centrifuge the sonicated samples for 10 min at 10,000 × g and 4°C.
Transfer 350 μL of the supernatant into a new 1.5 mL tube.
Do not touch the pellet during supernatant removal to avoid contamination with solid material.
Thaw frozen supernatant samples on ice if immediate activity detection is preferred.
Create a standard curve using 4-nitrophenol by performing serial 1:2 dilutions down to approximately 1 μM.
Detect fecal protein concentrations in the supernatants using any commercially available protein concentration detection kit.
Use LB buffer as blank and subtract detected absorption from sample absorption.
Calculate volume needed from each sample to achieve required fecal protein amounts for enzyme detection.
Add DB buffer into the respective wells of a 96-well plate to obtain a final volume of 150 μl per well.
Transfer required volumes of fecal protein solutions into respective wells.
Add substrate solutions (kit component 1) to the wells.
Detect absorption at 405 nm for 2–4 h at 37°C with 1–2 min detection intervals and a shaking step before each detection.
Prepare mouse and human fecal samples as described in step B.
Use 1 μg of total fecal protein for detection of α-galactosidase and β-N-acetyl-glucosaminidase activity.
Use 5 μg of total fecal protein for detection of β-glucosidase and α-fucosidase activity.
Use 25 μg of total fecal protein for detection of sulfatase activity.
Store mouse fecal samples at -20°C until preparation.
Obtain human stool samples from healthy volunteer donors.
Store human stool samples at -80°C until preparation.
Determine activities of all five enzymes with varying substrate concentrations for each individual.
Detect α-galactosidase, β-glucosidase, α-fucosidase, and sulfatase activity for substrate concentrations ranging from 1.25 mM to 40 mM.
Detect β-N-acetyl-glucosaminidase activity for substrate concentrations ranging from 0.31 mM to 10 mM.
Plot substrate turnover velocity (Vn) against substrate concentration for each enzyme.
Determine Vmax of every enzyme using standard Michaelis-Menten regression analysis.
Normalize all Vn of each individual and tested enzyme to Vmax of the respective individual and tested enzyme (% Vmax).
Determine optimal substrate concentrations for the detection of all 5 tested enzymes in mouse samples.
Determine optimal substrate concentrations for the detection of all 5 tested enzymes in human samples.
Note that α-fucosidase activities decrease with substrate concentrations exceeding approximately 15 mM N-FP.
Observe that sulfatase activities remain largely independent of substrate concentration within the tested range.
